papers.title: EXPRESS: Incentive Design for Sales Managers: Impact on Resource Allocation and Performance
papers.authors: Aritra Bhattacharya, Raghu Bommaraju, Rob Waiser
papers.abstract:
Many firms struggle to design effective incentives for sales
                    managers
                    . Yet despite a vast literature on salespeople’s incentives, little theoretical or empirical research has examined managers’ incentive structures. The authors address a common dilemma that firms face: Should managers’ incentives be based on achieving an
                    aggregate
                    target (
                    Aggregate Target Scheme
                    , ATS) or instead be linked to the target achievement of each
                    individual
                    territory or salesperson (
                    Individual Target Scheme
                    , ITS)? A quasi-experiment reveals that, despite ATS’s flexibility and apparent alignment with firm objectives, an ATS-to-ITS transition
                    improved performance
                    , with larger gains among lower-performing and higher-span territories. A scenario-based experiment with sales managers suggests that these effects may stem from the
                    reallocation
                    of resources from high to low performers but provides no evidence of an increase in managers’ overall resource investment. A survey of sales leaders indicates that a
                    sales star bias
                    —a managerial tendency to overallocate resources toward high performers relative to their marginal returns—likely drives suboptimal resource allocation under the flexible ATS. Finally, a supplementary field study documents that, following an ATS-to-ITS transition, managers increased
                    joint fieldwork
                    , especially with the lowest performers, and performance again improved. These results provide insights into managerial incentive design and offer guidance for firms.

papers.authors: Amandeep Singh, Kartik Hosanagar, Amit Gandhi
papers.abstract: A machine learning framework for constructing strong instrumental variables from weak exogenous data achieves semiparametric efficiency with applications to advertising and demand estimation.

papers.title: The Problem of Ignoring the Ignorability Assumption in Advertising Measurement: A Matrix Completion Solution
papers.abstract: This paper frames the overlap violation problem in online advertising auctions as a missing-data problem and proposes a matrix completion approach to correct the resulting bias in observational studies with algorithmic ad allocation.

papers.title: Frontiers: Reducing Disparity Between LLMs and Humans: Optimal LLM Sample Calibration
papers.authors: Yan Leng, Yunxin Sang, Ashish Agarwal
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to measure human preferences and opinions, but their outputs can diverge from human responses. We introduce human mimicry calibration (HuMCal), a post hoc, model-agnostic method that uses aggregate human benchmark data to learn how to combine LLM outputs from different prompts, personas, and model checkpoints. In applications to consumer transaction data and public opinion surveys, HuMCal improves agreement with human benchmarks over standard aggregation rules, and the calibrated weights often remain useful across time, geography, industry, and question clusters.

papers.title: Injunctive Norms Outperform Reciprocity: Tip Request Messages Can Increase Tipping Without Reducing Demand
papers.authors: Seung Hyun Kim, On Amir, Kenneth C. Wilbur
papers.abstract: Tip request messages are marketing communications that can help digital platforms balance customer spending with worker effort and compensation. We report the first field experiments testing how three appeals based on tipping motivations—injunctive norms (“It’s customary to leave a tip for the seller’s service”), personalized reciprocity, and impersonal reciprocity—affect tipping and future demand in a global freelance marketplace. Overall, the norms message increased tipping the most, and did so without reducing returning demand, showing that tip request messages can motivate customer tipping to better incentivize and compensate gig workers.
